newsitem.title: USA: Clinton builds big lead over Dole -- Reuters poll.
newsitem.headline: Clinton builds big lead over Dole -- Reuters poll.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, Political Correspondent

President Bill Clinton has built a 15-percentage-point lead over Republican Bob Dole in the 1996 presidential race and his dominance suggests the possibility of a rout, a Reuters poll showed on Thursday.

The poll of 1,019 likely voters was conducted for Reuters by John Zogby Group International between Sept(ember) 2-4. It found Clinton received a double boost, first from last week's Democratic convention and then from his decision to order air strikes against Iraq. The survey carried a margin of error of plus or minus 3.2 percentage points.

With two months to go to Election Day on November 5, Clinton led Dole by 48.2 percent to 33.3 percent. Texas billionaire Ross Perot, running at the head of his own Reform Party, had 5.9 percent. Other candidates polled 1.9 percent, and 10.6 percent said they were still undecided.
Surveys conducted in early September have been highly predictive of the eventual winner in past elections.

The poll showed Clinton had totally erased the boost Dole received from last month's Republican convention. In a previous Reuters poll conducted August 18-20 the week after the convention, Clinton's lead had been down to five points.
Clinton now leads among every income group, every ethnic group, every age group and in every region of the country. He leads by 10 points among men and 19 points among women.

"As the campaign officially starts, this is an impressive lead for Clinton, and given his remarkable dominance among most sub-groups, this has the potential for a rout similar to those in 1964, 1972 and 1984," said pollster John Zogby.

President Lyndon Johnson swamped Republican Barry Goldwater in 1964, winning over 61 percent of the popular vote. Presidents Richard Nixon and Ronald Reagan each won 49 of the 50 states in their election triumphs of 1972 and 1984.
Three other key indicators also show Clinton's prospects are bright. His personal favourability rating is at 61 percent, compared to 50.4 percent for Dole.

For the first time in Reuters polls, over half of those questioned said Clinton deserved re-election. And slightly more see the country headed in the right direction than think it is on the wrong track.
The president clearly benefitted both from the Democratic convention, from which he gained a six-point bounce, and from the Iraqi air raids which gave him a major boost on Tuesday.

While 61 percent of respondents said the strikes would not affect their vote, 26 percent said the action made them more inclined to support Clinton, while nine percent said it made them less likely to back him.

Conversely, the resignation of Clinton campaign strategist Dick Morris following allegations he shared confidential White House information with a prostitute had little impact on voters. Almost 80 percent of respondents said it would make no difference to their vote while 13 percent said it made them less likely to back Clinton.
The president's advantage was particularly impressive among independent voters, where he led Dole 50 to 19 percent.

Clinton's dominance was also clear on the top issues of the campaign. Voters gave him higher marks than Dole on handling the deficit (38-31 percent), the economy (42-28 percent), crime (38-34 percent), education (55-25 percent), health care (49-28 percent), the environment (51-19 percent), abortion (42-28 percent) and tobacco (46-21 percent).
Dole only led the president on foreign policy (42-35 percent) and character and integrity (45-28 percent).

Clinton's strength has also boosted Democratic prospects of regaining control of the Congress. In previous Reuters polls, a majority expressed a desire that Republicans retain control of both houses. This time, the Democrats were narrowly in the lead.

Most worrying for Dole, Clinton now leads by seven points even in the South, which should be a Republican stronghold. The president's lead in the West is back to 10 points and he leads by 15 points in the crucial Great Lakes/Central region where most analysts believe the election will be decided.
Clinton's position seems unassailable in the Northeast where he leads Dole 55-27 percent.
